[p. 496] Surah al-Qadr is Meccan, and it has five verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree.﴾ ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.﴾ ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein by the permission of their Lord, with every matter.﴾ ﴿It is peace until the emergence of dawn.﴾

This surah is Medinan according to the majority opinion, but al-Mawardi reported the opposite. Al-Wahidi mentioned that it was the first surah revealed in Medina. In a hadith: "Four people worshipped Allah, the Exalted, for eighty years without disobeying Him for the blink of an eye: Ayyub, Zakariyya, Hizqil and Yusha'." The Companions were amazed at this, so he recited ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ and the surah, and they were reassured by it. Its connection to what precedes it is clear: when He said ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-Alaq: 1], it was as if He said: Recite what We have sent down to you of Our words, ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree.﴾ The pronoun refers to what the meaning indicates, which is the pronoun for the Qur'an.

Ibn Abbas and others said: Allah sent it down entirely to the lowest heaven on the Night of Decree, then it was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) piecemeal over twenty years. Al-Sha'bi and others said: "Indeed, We began sending down this Qur'an to you during the Night of Decree." It was also reported that the angel's descent to Hira' occurred in the last ten nights of Ramadan. It was said that the meaning is: We sent down this surah concerning the Night of Decree and its excellence. Since the surah is part of the Qur'an, the pronoun refers to the Qur'an for the sake of magnification and beautification. Thus the Night of Decree is not a time-frame (zarf) for the revelation; rather, it is like the saying of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I feared that a Qur'an might be revealed concerning me," and the saying of Aisha: "I consider myself too insignificant for a Qur'an to be revealed concerning me." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It magnifies the Qur'an by attributing its sending down to Me exclusively, and by its being referred to by a pronoun rather than an explicit noun, as a testimony to its prominence and to its needing no indication, and by raising the status of the time in which it was sent down." End of quote. There is some abridgment in it.

The Night was named Laylat al-Qadr because in it the lifespans, provisions and all events of the world are decreed and handed over to the angels to carry out. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatada and others. Al-Zuhri said: its meaning is the Night of great honour and nobility; "greatness of status" derives from your saying: "a man who has qadr (status)." Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: it was named so because it bestows great status upon whoever revives it, a status he did not have before, and it makes him great in the sight of Allah, the Exalted. It was also said: it was named so because all the deeds performed in it have value and worth. It was said: because He sent down in it a Book of great worth, upon a Messenger of great worth, to a community of great worth. It was said: because in it angels of great worth and status descend. It was said: because He decreed mercy for the believers in it. Al-Khalil said: because the earth becomes constricted (yadiq) by the angels in it, as in His saying ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted (qudira)﴾ [al-Talaq: 7], meaning constricted. The early and later scholars differed greatly and in conflicting ways in determining its time. Some said it has been lifted, but what the hadith indicates is that it has not been lifted, that it is in the last ten nights, and that it is on the odd nights, as the Prayer and Peace be upon him said: "Seek it on the twenty-first, the twenty-third, the twenty-fifth, the twenty-seventh and the twenty-ninth." In the Sahih: "Whoever stands in prayer on the Night of Decree in faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven."

﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ is an expression of its magnificence, meaning: your knowledge does not reach the full extent of its excellence. Then He explained it to him. Sufyan ibn Uyayna said: whatever in the Qur'an comes as "And what can make you know" (wa ma adraka), He has informed him of it; but whatever comes as "And what can make you know" (wa ma yudrika), He has not informed him of it. It was said: Allah concealed it from His servants so that they would strive in worship and not rely on its excellence while neglecting other times. Apparently ﴿a thousand months﴾ is intended literally as a number, which is eighty years and three years. Al-Hasan said: the Night of Decree is better than acting in these months. The meaning is: ﴿better than a thousand months﴾ devoid of the Night of Decree, and this is the view of most exegetes. Abu al-Aliya said: better than a thousand months of Ramadan in which there is no Night of Decree. It was also said: the meaning is better than the whole of time, because the Arabs mention "a thousand" to denote the extremity of all things. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Each of them would love to be granted a life of a thousand years﴾ [al-Baqara: 96], meaning the whole of time. Al-Hasan ibn Ali was reproached for handing over the affair to Muawiya, and he said: Allah, the Exalted, showed His Prophet (ﷺ) in a dream the Banu Umayya leaping upon his grave like monkeys, and he was distressed by this, so Allah gave him the Night of Decree, which is better than the period of the kings of the Banu Umayya, and informed him that they would rule for this length of time. Al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl al-Judhami said: "We counted that, and it came to exactly a thousand months, not exceeding a day nor falling short by a day." Al-Tirmidhi transmitted something close to this meaning and said: "It is a gharib hadith." End of quote.

It was said: the last of their kings was Marwan al-Ja'di at the end of this period of time. This is not contradicted by the Banu Umayya ruling in al-Andalus for a period other than this, because they were in a remote part of the earth and at the far edge of Arab settlement, where there were many other kings in the Arab region at that time. It was also mentioned, regarding the specification of this period, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned a man from the Children of Israel who wore weapons in the way of Allah for a thousand months, so the believers were amazed at this and their own deeds seemed small to them, so they were given a night better than the duration of that warrior. It was also said: in the past, a man was not called "a worshipper" until he had worshipped Allah, the Exalted, for a thousand months, so they were given a night which, if they revive it, they are more entitled to be called worshippers than those worshippers. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: Sulayman and Dhu al-Qarnayn each ruled for five hundred years, which makes a thousand months, so Allah made the deed in this night for whoever attains it better than their kingdom.

﴿The angels and the Spirit descend﴾: the disagreement concerning the Spirit has already been mentioned: is it Jibril, or a mercy with which he descends, or another angel, or the most honoured of the angels, or a host other than them, or guardians over other angels? The descent (tanazzul) is either to the earth or to the lowest heaven. ﴿By the permission of their Lord﴾ is connected to "descend." ﴿With every matter﴾ is also connected to "descend," and "min" (from) is causal: meaning they descend on account of every matter that Allah has decreed for that year until the next. ﴿It is peace﴾ is a new sentence, a predicate (khabar) of the subject (mubtada') which is "hiya" (it), meaning: it is peace until the beginning of its dawn. This was said by Abu al-Aliya, Nafi' al-Muqri and al-Farra'. This is according to the view of those who said that their descent is to decree the affairs for them. Abu Hatim said: "min" here means "bi" (with), meaning "with every matter." Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and al-Kalbi said: "from every man," meaning on account of every person. It was also said that "every man" refers to the angels, meaning from every angel a greeting upon the believers who are occupied in worship. Abu Hatim rejected this view. ﴿It is peace﴾: meaning it is peace, made peace because of the abundance of peace in it. It was said: they do not meet a believing man or woman without greeting them in that night. Mansur and al-Sha'bi said: "peace" means greeting, meaning the angels greet the believers. As for those who said that their descent is not for the decreeing of affairs in that year, they made the sentence complete at His saying "by the permission of their Lord," and said: "with every matter" is connected to His saying "it is peace," meaning: peace from every frightening matter from which one should be safe. Mujahid said: no disease afflicts anyone in it. Sahib al-Lawami' said: it was also said that its meaning is: it is peace from every matter, and "my matter" (amri) is safe or secured from it. It is not permissible for "peace" in this apparent wording, which is a verbal noun (masdar), to govern what precedes it, because it is impermissible to front a complement (ma'mul) of a verbal noun before the verbal noun, just as the relative clause (sila) cannot be placed before the relative pronoun (mawsul). End of quote.

From Ibn Abbas: the sentence is complete at His saying "peace," and the word "hiya" (it) is an indication that it is the twenty-seventh night of the month, since this word "hiya" is the twenty-seventh word of the words of this surah. End of quote. Such a thing is not authentically transmitted from Ibn Abbas; it is rather a kind of riddle, and the speech of Allah, the Exalted, is far above that.

The majority read "matla'i" (the rising) with a fatha on the lam. Abu Raja', al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab, Talha, Ibn Muhaysin, al-Kisa'i and Abu Amr, in one of the reports from him, read it with a kasra. It was said: both are verbal nouns in the dialect of the Banu Tamim. It was also said: the verbal noun is with a fatha, and the place of rising with a kasra according to the people of the Hijaz.

[p. 496] Surah al-Qadr is Meccan, and it has five verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree.﴾ ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.﴾ ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein by the permission of their Lord, with every matter.﴾ ﴿It is peace until the emergence of dawn.﴾

This surah is Medinan according to the majority opinion, but al-Mawardi reported the opposite. Al-Wahidi mentioned that it was the first surah revealed in Medina. In a hadith: "Four people worshipped Allah, the Exalted, for eighty years without disobeying Him for the blink of an eye: Ayyub, Zakariyya, Hizqil and Yusha'." The Companions were amazed at this, so he recited ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ and the surah, and they were reassured by it. Its connection to what precedes it is clear: when He said ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-Alaq: 1], it was as if He said: Recite what We have sent down to you of Our words, ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree.﴾ The pronoun refers to what the meaning indicates, which is the pronoun for the Qur'an.

Ibn Abbas and others said: Allah sent it down entirely to the lowest heaven on the Night of Decree, then it was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) piecemeal over twenty years. Al-Sha'bi and others said: "Indeed, We began sending down this Qur'an to you during the Night of Decree." It was also reported that the angel's descent to Hira' occurred in the last ten nights of Ramadan. It was said that the meaning is: We sent down this surah concerning the Night of Decree and its excellence. Since the surah is part of the Qur'an, the pronoun refers to the Qur'an for the sake of magnification and beautification. Thus the Night of Decree is not a time-frame (zarf) for the revelation; rather, it is like the saying of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I feared that a Qur'an might be revealed concerning me," and the saying of Aisha: "I consider myself too insignificant for a Qur'an to be revealed concerning me." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It magnifies the Qur'an by attributing its sending down to Me exclusively, and by its being referred to by a pronoun rather than an explicit noun, as a testimony to its prominence and to its needing no indication, and by raising the status of the time in which it was sent down." End of quote. There is some abridgment in it.

The Night was named Laylat al-Qadr because in it the lifespans, provisions and all events of the world are decreed and handed over to the angels to carry out. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatada and others. Al-Zuhri said: its meaning is the Night of great honour and nobility; "greatness of status" derives from your saying: "a man who has qadr (status)." Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: it was named so because it bestows great status upon whoever revives it, a status he did not have before, and it makes him great in the sight of Allah, the Exalted. It was also said: it was named so because all the deeds performed in it have value and worth. It was said: because He sent down in it a Book of great worth, upon a Messenger of great worth, to a community of great worth. It was said: because in it angels of great worth and status descend. It was said: because He decreed mercy for the believers in it. Al-Khalil said: because the earth becomes constricted (yadiq) by the angels in it, as in His saying ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted (qudira)﴾ [al-Talaq: 7], meaning constricted. The early and later scholars differed greatly and in conflicting ways in determining its time. Some said it has been lifted, but what the hadith indicates is that it has not been lifted, that it is in the last ten nights, and that it is on the odd nights, as the Prayer and Peace be upon him said: "Seek it on the twenty-first, the twenty-third, the twenty-fifth, the twenty-seventh and the twenty-ninth." In the Sahih: "Whoever stands in prayer on the Night of Decree in faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven."

﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ is an expression of its magnificence, meaning: your knowledge does not reach the full extent of its excellence. Then He explained it to him. Sufyan ibn Uyayna said: whatever in the Qur'an comes as "And what can make you know" (wa ma adraka), He has informed him of it; but whatever comes as "And what can make you know" (wa ma yudrika), He has not informed him of it. It was said: Allah concealed it from His servants so that they would strive in worship and not rely on its excellence while neglecting other times. Apparently ﴿a thousand months﴾ is intended literally as a number, which is eighty years and three years. Al-Hasan said: the Night of Decree is better than acting in these months. The meaning is: ﴿better than a thousand months﴾ devoid of the Night of Decree, and this is the view of most exegetes. Abu al-Aliya said: better than a thousand months of Ramadan in which there is no Night of Decree. It was also said: the meaning is better than the whole of time, because the Arabs mention "a thousand" to denote the extremity of all things. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Each of them would love to be granted a life of a thousand years﴾ [al-Baqara: 96], meaning the whole of time. Al-Hasan ibn Ali was reproached for handing over the affair to Muawiya, and he said: Allah, the Exalted, showed His Prophet (ﷺ) in a dream the Banu Umayya leaping upon his grave like monkeys, and he was distressed by this, so Allah gave him the Night of Decree, which is better than the period of the kings of the Banu Umayya, and informed him that they would rule for this length of time. Al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl al-Judhami said: "We counted that, and it came to exactly a thousand months, not exceeding a day nor falling short by a day." Al-Tirmidhi transmitted something close to this meaning and said: "It is a gharib hadith." End of quote.

It was said: the last of their kings was Marwan al-Ja'di at the end of this period of time. This is not contradicted by the Banu Umayya ruling in al-Andalus for a period other than this, because they were in a remote part of the earth and at the far edge of Arab settlement, where there were many other kings in the Arab region at that time. It was also mentioned, regarding the specification of this period, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned a man from the Children of Israel who wore weapons in the way of Allah for a thousand months, so the believers were amazed at this and their own deeds seemed small to them, so they were given a night better than the duration of that warrior. It was also said: in the past, a man was not called "a worshipper" until he had worshipped Allah, the Exalted, for a thousand months, so they were given a night which, if they revive it, they are more entitled to be called worshippers than those worshippers. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: Sulayman and Dhu al-Qarnayn each ruled for five hundred years, which makes a thousand months, so Allah made the deed in this night for whoever attains it better than their kingdom.

﴿The angels and the Spirit descend﴾: the disagreement concerning the Spirit has already been mentioned: is it Jibril, or a mercy with which he descends, or another angel, or the most honoured of the angels, or a host other than them, or guardians over other angels? The descent (tanazzul) is either to the earth or to the lowest heaven. ﴿By the permission of their Lord﴾ is connected to "descend." ﴿With every matter﴾ is also connected to "descend," and "min" (from) is causal: meaning they descend on account of every matter that Allah has decreed for that year until the next. ﴿It is peace﴾ is a new sentence, a predicate (khabar) of the subject (mubtada') which is "hiya" (it), meaning: it is peace until the beginning of its dawn. This was said by Abu al-Aliya, Nafi' al-Muqri and al-Farra'. This is according to the view of those who said that their descent is to decree the affairs for them. Abu Hatim said: "min" here means "bi" (with), meaning "with every matter." Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and al-Kalbi said: "from every man," meaning on account of every person. It was also said that "every man" refers to the angels, meaning from every angel a greeting upon the believers who are occupied in worship. Abu Hatim rejected this view. ﴿It is peace﴾: meaning it is peace, made peace because of the abundance of peace in it. It was said: they do not meet a believing man or woman without greeting them in that night. Mansur and al-Sha'bi said: "peace" means greeting, meaning the angels greet the believers. As for those who said that their descent is not for the decreeing of affairs in that year, they made the sentence complete at His saying "by the permission of their Lord," and said: "with every matter" is connected to His saying "it is peace," meaning: peace from every frightening matter from which one should be safe. Mujahid said: no disease afflicts anyone in it. Sahib al-Lawami' said: it was also said that its meaning is: it is peace from every matter, and "my matter" (amri) is safe or secured from it. It is not permissible for "peace" in this apparent wording, which is a verbal noun (masdar), to govern what precedes it, because it is impermissible to front a complement (ma'mul) of a verbal noun before the verbal noun, just as the relative clause (sila) cannot be placed before the relative pronoun (mawsul). End of quote.
